question: Your interactive support assistant and a nightly job that summarizes 40,000 tickets both call the same Global Standard chat model deployment in a Microsoft Foundry project. Every night the batch job saturates the deployment's tokens-per-minute quota: the batch sees continuous 429 responses and the interactive app's p95 latency jumps from 1.2 s to 9 s. What is the most appropriate change?
options: Create a separate deployment for the offline summarization job using the Batch deployment type, and leave the interactive traffic on its own Standard deployment with its own quota allocation
Keep the single deployment and add exponential backoff with jitter to the batch client so that it retries 429s until the nightly run finishes
Switch the interactive app to a smaller model so each interactive request consumes fewer tokens per minute from the shared quota
Move both workloads onto one Provisioned Throughput deployment sized for the batch job's peak token rate so that capacity is reserved
optionExplanations: Correct. Quota is enforced per deployment, so the only way to stop one workload starving another is to give them separate deployments. The offline job has no interactive latency requirement, so the Batch deployment type processes it asynchronously at lower cost while the Standard deployment keeps its full token budget for live users.

Backoff is good hygiene and the batch job needs it regardless, but it does not create capacity. The retries still consume the same shared quota, so the interactive app keeps queueing behind batch traffic and the p95 latency spike persists every night.

This misreads the failure: the interactive app is the victim, not the cause. Shrinking its token footprint frees a little quota but the batch job will simply absorb it, and you have degraded answer quality for live users without isolating the two workloads.

Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity, but sizing it for the batch peak means paying for that reserved capacity 24 hours a day, and a single shared deployment still lets the batch job consume the whole reservation. Isolation, not reservation, is what this problem needs.
principle: quota is enforced per deployment, so isolate workloads with different latency profiles
relatedConcept: Foundry deployment types — Standard, Global Standard, Data Zone, Provisioned and Batch — differ in latency guarantees, data residency and billing, and each deployment carries its own rate limits.
overallExplanation: Give the offline job its own Batch deployment and keep interactive traffic on a dedicated Standard deployment. Rate limits apply per deployment, so co-locating a bursty batch workload with latency-sensitive traffic guarantees contention no matter how carefully the batch client retries.

question: A field-service platform classifies about 2 million short maintenance notes per day into a fixed taxonomy of 12 fault categories. It currently sends each note to a large frontier reasoning model, which costs far more than the team's budget allows and averages 3.1 s per note. Accuracy on a labelled sample is 96%, and a fine-tuned small model reaches 95% on the same sample. What should you deploy?
options: Deploy a small language model from the Foundry model catalog for the bulk classification path, and route only the rare free-text escalation summaries to the large model
Keep the frontier reasoning model but set its reasoning effort to the lowest setting and temperature to 0 so that responses are shorter and cheaper
Keep the frontier model and add a response cache keyed on the exact note text so that repeated notes skip the model entirely
Replace the classifier with a multimodal model, because technicians sometimes attach photographs to the maintenance notes
optionExplanations: Correct. A closed 12-label taxonomy over short text is exactly the workload small language models are sized for, and losing one accuracy point buys an order-of-magnitude reduction in cost and latency at 2 million calls a day. Keeping the large model for the small volume of open-ended summaries preserves quality where judgement is genuinely required.

Lower reasoning effort trims output tokens but you still pay frontier per-token pricing for every one of the 2 million notes, and the per-request overhead of a large model keeps latency high. Parameter tuning cannot close an order-of-magnitude unit-cost gap.

Caching helps only to the extent that note text repeats verbatim, which free-typed technician notes rarely do. It leaves the cost of every cache miss unchanged, so it is a marginal optimization rather than a fix for the wrong model choice.

This changes the modality without addressing cost or latency, and multimodal models are more expensive per request than text-only models. Photograph handling is a separate requirement that should be solved on its own path, not by upgrading the bulk text classifier.
principle: match model size to task complexity, not to the most capable model available
relatedConcept: The Foundry model catalog spans frontier LLMs, small language models, code models and multimodal models; high-volume, narrow tasks are usually the ones where a small model wins on cost and latency.
overallExplanation: Use a small language model for the high-volume fixed-taxonomy classification and reserve the frontier model for the rare open-ended work. Matching model capability to task complexity is the single biggest lever on cost and latency in a production generative application.

question: A Python app lets customers photograph a damaged parcel and asks a multimodal model deployment to describe the visible damage. The developer builds the request as messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Describe the damage: " + base64_image}] and the model replies that it cannot see any image and appears to treat the base64 blob as text. What is the correct fix?
options: Send content as a list of typed content parts — a text part with the instruction and an image part carrying the picture as a data URL or an accessible HTTPS URL
Prefix the base64 string with "data:image/jpeg;base64," inside the same text string so that the model recognizes the encoding
Run the image through an OCR step first and pass the extracted text to the model, because chat completions accept text only
Upload the photograph to the Foundry project's file store and reference it by file name in the prompt text so that the deployment resolves it
optionExplanations: Correct. Multimodal chat requests represent a single user turn as an array of content parts, each with its own type. The image must travel in an image content part — as a data URL or a URL the service can fetch — so the service routes it to the vision encoder rather than tokenizing it as characters.

The data URL prefix is required inside an image content part, but adding it to a plain text string changes nothing structurally: the value is still a text part, so the model still receives characters, not pixels. The problem is the content type, not the encoding header.

This encodes the misconception that chat completions are text-only. Multimodal deployments accept images natively, and OCR would discard exactly the information the scenario needs — dents, tears and crushed corners are visual damage, not text on the box.

There is no mechanism by which a chat deployment resolves a bare file name mentioned in prompt text into image bytes. Storing the file is fine, but the request must still carry either the bytes as a data URL or a URL the service can retrieve.
principle: images travel as typed content parts, not as text in the prompt string
relatedConcept: Consuming multimodal deployments means constructing multi-part message content, where each part declares whether it is text, an image or another supported modality.
overallExplanation: Build the user message as a list of content parts with a separate image part carrying a data URL or fetchable URL. Pasting base64 into the text string leaves the payload as tokens, which is why the model reports that it sees no image.

question: Your RAG assistant retrieves from an Azure AI Search index of 180,000 HR policy chunks using pure vector search with top-k of 5. Questions that quote an exact policy identifier such as "What does HR-4417 say about carry-over leave?" return semantically similar but wrong policies, and the groundedness evaluator averages 0.62 on that query class. Which two retrieval changes should you make? (Choose two.)
options: Enable hybrid retrieval so that the keyword (BM25) side of the query matches the literal identifier alongside the vector similarity side
Add semantic ranking over a larger candidate set, so the top 50 hybrid candidates are re-scored and only the best few reach the prompt
Raise the generation temperature to 0.9 so the model explores more of the retrieved context before answering
Increase top-k to 100 and pass every retrieved chunk into the prompt so the correct policy is guaranteed to be present
optionExplanations: Correct. Embeddings blur rare literal tokens such as "HR-4417", which is precisely why a semantically close but incorrect policy wins. Hybrid search runs keyword and vector retrieval together and fuses the results, so exact identifiers are matched lexically while natural-language phrasing is still matched semantically.

Correct. Semantic ranking re-scores a wide candidate list with a deeper relevance model, so recall can be raised by retrieving more candidates without polluting the prompt. Retrieve broadly, rerank, then pass only the top few chunks — that is the standard fix for good recall with poor precision at the top.

Temperature governs sampling of the model's output tokens; it has no effect on which documents are retrieved. Raising it on a grounded question-answering task increases the chance of fabricated detail, so this would push groundedness down rather than up.

Flooding the prompt with 100 chunks raises cost and latency and dilutes attention across mostly irrelevant text, which typically lowers answer quality. Retrieval precision, not prompt volume, is the lever here — and the wrong-policy chunks would still be present to mislead the model.
principle: hybrid retrieval plus reranking fixes exact-token recall that embeddings alone lose
relatedConcept: Grounding quality in RAG is determined mostly at the retrieval stage; hybrid search with semantic reranking is the default configuration for mixed natural-language and identifier queries.
overallExplanation: Turn on hybrid (keyword + vector) retrieval and add semantic reranking over a wider candidate set. Exact identifiers are lexical signals that embeddings smooth away, and reranking lets you retrieve broadly while still sending the model a small, precise context.

question: A RAG assistant over machine-maintenance manuals answers procedural questions with steps that stop halfway, and citations often point at a chunk that begins mid-sentence. Ingestion splits each PDF into fixed 4,000-token chunks with no overlap, discarding heading structure, so a single procedure or table is frequently cut across two chunks. What should you change first?
options: Re-chunk the manuals along document structure into smaller, semantically coherent units with overlap, carrying section headings as chunk metadata
Move to a model with a larger context window so that more of the manual fits into each request
Set temperature to 0 so the model stops inventing the missing half of each procedure
Embed each complete manual as a single vector so that no procedure can ever be split across chunks
optionExplanations: Correct. The defect is created at ingestion: a retrieval unit that begins mid-sentence and ends mid-procedure cannot ground a complete answer no matter what the model does. Structure-aware chunking with overlap keeps each procedure intact, and heading metadata gives both the ranker and the model the context a fragment otherwise loses.

A larger context window lets you pass more chunks, but every chunk is still a truncated fragment. You would be paying for more tokens to carry the same broken retrieval units, and the truncated-procedure symptom would remain.

Temperature affects output sampling, not what the retriever supplies. With half a procedure in context, a deterministic model simply produces the same incomplete answer every time — the grounding gap is upstream of generation.

One vector per manual destroys retrieval precision: a single embedding cannot represent hundreds of pages, so the retriever loses the ability to locate the specific procedure. This trades a chunking bug for a far worse recall problem.
principle: the chunk is the unit of grounding, so chunk on meaning, not on a fixed token count
relatedConcept: RAG ingestion decisions — chunk size, overlap, structure awareness and retained metadata — bound the best answer quality any downstream model can achieve.
overallExplanation: Re-chunk along document structure with overlap and preserve heading metadata. Truncated answers with mid-sentence citations are an ingestion defect, and no model parameter or larger context window repairs a retrieval unit that never contained the whole procedure.

question: Auditors testing your grounded benefits assistant find that when the search index returns no matching chunk — for example for a benefit the company does not offer — the assistant still produces a fluent, confident, entirely invented answer with no citation. Retrieval scores for those queries are far below the scores seen on answerable questions. What is the most effective mitigation?
options: Gate on the retrieval score in application code and, when no chunk clears the threshold, either skip the model call or pass an empty-context prompt whose instructions require an explicit "not covered in the provided sources" reply with citations otherwise mandatory
Set temperature and top_p to 0 so that the assistant's answers become deterministic and therefore factual
Fine-tune the model on 5,000 historical benefits questions and answers so it learns the company's actual benefits catalogue
Increase top-k from 5 to 20 so that there is always some context for the model to ground its answer in
optionExplanations: Correct. Fabrication on unanswerable questions is a control-flow problem as much as a prompting problem: the application must recognize that retrieval failed and must define what the assistant says in that state. A score threshold in code plus instructions that mandate citations and an explicit abstention response gives the model a sanctioned way to say nothing.

Determinism is not accuracy. A temperature of 0 makes the assistant invent the same fabricated benefit on every run, which is arguably worse for auditors because the failure now looks reproducible and authoritative.

Fine-tuning bakes a snapshot of the catalogue into weights that drift the moment benefits change, and it still gives the model no signal that a particular question is unanswerable. It also does not produce the citations the audit requires.

Retrieving 20 chunks when zero are relevant simply supplies 20 irrelevant chunks, which invites the model to stitch an answer from unrelated policies. Raising top-k addresses recall, not the abstention behaviour the auditors flagged.
principle: an assistant needs a sanctioned way to say "I don't know"
relatedConcept: Detecting and preventing fabrication in RAG combines retrieval-score gating in application code with instructions that require citations and permit explicit abstention.
overallExplanation: Check the retrieval score before generating and require an explicit abstention response, with citations mandatory otherwise. Fabrication on unanswerable questions is fixed by giving the system a defined empty-retrieval path, not by tightening sampling parameters.

question: An invoice-processing solution must always run the same three stages: extract fields from the PDF, validate totals and vendor identifiers against the ERP, then post the invoice. A developer proposes giving a single model all three capabilities as tools and letting it decide the order each run. Finance requires that no invoice is ever posted before validation succeeds. How should the flow be designed?
options: Orchestrate the three stages as a deterministic workflow in application code, calling the model only for the extraction stage where judgement is required
Keep the model-driven design but add a system instruction stating that validation must always precede posting
Keep the model-driven design and lower temperature to 0 so the model always chooses the same tool order
Let the model plan freely and add a post-run evaluator that flags any invoice posted before validation so finance can reverse it
optionExplanations: Correct. The stage order is fixed, known in advance and safety-critical, which is the definition of a workflow rather than an agent. Encoding the sequence in code makes the ordering guarantee structural, while the model still does the one genuinely probabilistic job — reading a messy PDF.

Instructions shape probabilities; they do not enforce invariants. A single unusual invoice, a prompt injection embedded in a PDF, or an ordinary sampling anomaly can still produce a post-before-validate sequence, which is exactly what finance said must never happen.

Temperature 0 reduces variability but is not a guarantee: the same deployment can still choose differently as inputs vary or as the deployed model version changes. Determinism of sampling is not the same as a hard ordering constraint.

Detecting the violation after the money has moved is a compensating control, not a prevention. Reversing posted invoices creates audit and reconciliation work that a five-line deterministic sequence in code would have avoided entirely.
principle: if the sequence is known in advance, it is a workflow, not an agent
relatedConcept: Designing generative solutions means separating deterministic orchestration, which belongs in code, from the specific steps where language understanding is actually needed.
overallExplanation: Implement the fixed three-stage sequence as a deterministic workflow and use the model only for extraction. Model instructions bias behaviour but cannot enforce a safety-critical ordering invariant; code can.

question: A quoting assistant handles one long prompt that reads a customer specification, applies tiered volume discounts and regional tax rules, and emits a formatted quote. Sales reports that about 12% of quotes contain arithmetic errors — discount tiers applied to the wrong subtotal, tax computed on the pre-discount amount — even though the extracted specification is correct. Which two changes best address this? (Choose two.)
options: Expose the pricing calculation as a deterministic tool the model calls with structured parameters, and have the tool, not the model, compute discounts and tax
Split the single prompt into discrete steps with a schema-validated hand-off, so extraction output is validated before it is passed to the pricing step
Lower the temperature from 0.2 to 0 so that the arithmetic becomes deterministic and therefore correct
Append "Please double-check all calculations carefully before answering" to the end of the system prompt
optionExplanations: Correct. Arithmetic over business rules is deterministic work that should never be sampled token by token. Moving the calculation into a tool means the model's job shrinks to identifying the right parameters, and the pricing logic becomes testable, auditable and exactly repeatable.

Correct. A single monolithic prompt hides where the failure occurs and lets a malformed intermediate value flow straight into pricing. Discrete steps with a validated schema between them localize the error, make each step independently testable, and stop bad extractions from silently corrupting downstream math.

This confuses determinism with correctness. Temperature 0 makes the model apply the discount to the wrong subtotal consistently rather than occasionally, which removes the variance that was making the bug visible without removing the bug.

Exhortations like this produce small, unreliable gains and no guarantee. A 12% error rate on money is a design defect, and prompt encouragement leaves the arithmetic in exactly the place — free-form generation — where it cannot be verified.
principle: deterministic computation belongs in a tool, not in generated tokens
relatedConcept: Tool-augmented and multistep reasoning pipelines work by narrowing the model to the language-understanding parts of the task and delegating exact computation and validation to code.
overallExplanation: Move the pricing math into a deterministic tool and break the monolithic prompt into schema-validated steps. Models are unreliable calculators; the fix is architectural — delegate exact computation to code and validate the hand-offs between stages.

question: An RFP assistant must answer eight independent sub-questions, each needing its own retrieval against a different index section, before composing a single response. The current implementation loops through the sub-questions one at a time, and end-to-end latency averages 22 s — roughly 2.5 s per sub-question plus a final composition call. Answers are accurate. What change reduces latency the most?
options: Issue the eight retrieval-and-generation calls concurrently with asyncio and then run one composition call over the collected results
Merge all eight sub-questions into one prompt with all retrieved context concatenated so only a single model call is needed
Enable response streaming so the user starts seeing tokens sooner while the eight sub-questions are still being processed
Increase max_tokens on each sub-question call so the model does not have to work as hard to stay within the limit
optionExplanations: Correct. The sub-questions are independent, so the sequential loop is spending 20 s waiting on I/O that could overlap. Running them concurrently collapses eight serial round trips into roughly one, and the final composition call still sees every result — accuracy is preserved while wall-clock time drops to near the slowest branch.

One giant prompt does cut round trips, but it concatenates eight retrieval sets into a single context, which dilutes attention and typically degrades per-question accuracy. The scenario states answers are currently accurate, so a change that risks that quality is the wrong trade.

Streaming improves perceived latency for the final composition only. The eight upstream calls must still finish before composition begins, so the user still waits roughly 20 s before the first token appears.

max_tokens caps output length; it does not make the model faster and it does not reduce the number of serial round trips. If anything, a larger cap permits longer generations and slightly higher per-call latency.
principle: independent steps should run concurrently, not in a loop
relatedConcept: Multistep generative pipelines are usually latency-bound on serialized I/O; fan-out then synthesize is the standard shape when sub-tasks do not depend on one another.
overallExplanation: Fan the eight independent sub-questions out concurrently and synthesize once at the end. Sequential loops over independent model calls waste wall-clock time on I/O waits, and unlike prompt merging, concurrency preserves the per-question accuracy you already have.

question: Before releasing a grounded clinical-policy assistant, you must produce evidence for the review board about how often the assistant asserts facts that its retrieved sources do not support. You have a set of 300 evaluation questions with the retrieved context captured for each, but no human-written reference answers. Which evaluator should you run?
options: The groundedness evaluator, scoring each response against the query and the retrieved context it was given
The relevance evaluator, scoring whether each response actually addresses the question that was asked
The coherence and fluency evaluators, since well-formed answers are less likely to contain fabricated claims
The similarity evaluator, comparing each response with the reference answer for that question
optionExplanations: Correct. Groundedness asks precisely the review board's question: is every claim in the response supported by the supplied context? It needs the query, the context and the response but no ground-truth answer, which matches the data you actually have.

Relevance measures whether the answer is on-topic for the question. A response can be perfectly relevant and still assert unsupported clinical facts, so relevance would miss exactly the failure mode under review.

Coherence and fluency measure readability and logical flow of the language. Fabrications are typically fluent and coherent — that is what makes them dangerous — so these evaluators provide no signal about factual support.

The similarity evaluator requires ground-truth reference answers, which this evaluation set does not have. It also penalizes valid paraphrases and rewards wording overlap, neither of which is a measure of source support.
principle: groundedness measures support by the context; relevance measures fit to the question
relatedConcept: Foundry's evaluators split into RAG metrics (groundedness, retrieval, relevance), general quality metrics (coherence, fluency), ground-truth metrics (similarity, F1) and safety evaluators.
overallExplanation: Run the groundedness evaluator over query, context and response. It is the metric defined to detect claims unsupported by retrieved sources, and unlike similarity it needs no human-written reference answers.

question: A consumer-facing assistant is going to public preview and the risk committee wants quantitative evidence about how it behaves when users deliberately try to elicit harmful content or bypass its instructions. The team has content filters enabled at the deployment and a suite of quality evaluators, but no data on adversarial behaviour. What should you add before launch?
options: Run safety evaluations driven by the adversarial simulator, which generates attack and jailbreak prompts and scores responses for hateful, violent, sexual and self-harm content
Raise every content filter category to its strictest severity threshold and record the number of requests the filter blocks in production
Add the coherence, fluency and relevance evaluators to the release gate, since low-quality outputs correlate with unsafe outputs
Have two engineers spend a day writing about 20 hostile prompts by hand and review the responses in a meeting
optionExplanations: Correct. The committee asked for measurement under adversarial conditions, and that is what a simulator-driven safety evaluation produces: synthesized attack and jailbreak prompts run at scale, with per-category harm scores and defect rates you can trend release over release.

Content filters are a runtime mitigation, not a measurement. Tightening them without evaluation data trades unknown safety gains for known false-positive costs, and a production block count tells you nothing before launch.

Quality evaluators measure whether text reads well and answers the question. A jailbroken response is usually fluent, coherent and highly relevant to the attacker's request, so these metrics would look healthy while the risk remains unmeasured.

A manual red-team pass is valuable qualitative input but 20 hand-written prompts give no statistical coverage across harm categories and cannot be re-run automatically on each release to detect regressions.
principle: filters mitigate risk; evaluations measure it — a launch gate needs both
relatedConcept: Safety evaluation in Foundry pairs an adversarial simulator that synthesizes attack prompts with harm-category evaluators, producing repeatable defect rates rather than anecdotes.
overallExplanation: Run simulator-driven safety evaluations that generate adversarial and jailbreak prompts and score the responses by harm category. Content filters reduce risk at runtime but produce no pre-launch evidence, and quality evaluators are blind to harmful-but-fluent output.

question: Your RAG assistant scores 0.91 average groundedness across the evaluation set, yet a user study finds that roughly a quarter of answers are technically supported by their citations but do not answer what the user actually asked. Your evaluation pipeline currently measures groundedness and fluency only. What should you add to explain the gap?
options: Retrieval and relevance metrics, so you can tell whether the retrieved documents were the right ones for the query and whether the answer addresses the question
A higher groundedness pass threshold, raising the release gate from 0.80 to 0.95 so weakly supported answers fail
A larger generation model, since more capable models produce answers that better match user intent
A second groundedness run using a different judge model to confirm that the 0.91 score is reliable
optionExplanations: Correct. High groundedness with low usefulness is the signature of faithful answers built on the wrong documents. Splitting evaluation into a retrieval stage metric and a response relevance metric shows whether the retriever surfaced the right chunks and whether the final answer addresses the query — the two things groundedness deliberately does not measure.

Tightening the threshold on a metric that is already high just fails more answers for weak sourcing. The failing behaviour is well-sourced but off-target, so it would keep passing a stricter groundedness gate.

A larger model can only reason over the context it receives. If retrieval hands it the wrong policy or the wrong section, a more capable model produces a more articulate off-target answer, at higher cost.

Cross-checking with a second judge tests the reliability of the groundedness score, not its coverage. Even a perfectly calibrated groundedness score is silent on whether the answer addressed the user's question.
principle: evaluate retrieval and generation separately — grounded in the wrong document is still wrong
relatedConcept: RAG evaluation is two-stage: retrieval metrics judge whether the right context was found, generation metrics such as groundedness and relevance judge what the model did with it.
overallExplanation: Add retrieval-stage and response-relevance metrics alongside groundedness. An answer faithfully grounded in an irrelevant document scores well on groundedness and still fails the user, so the retrieval stage needs its own measurement.

question: A Python service running in containers on Azure Kubernetes Service currently reads an API key from an environment variable to call a Foundry model deployment. Security has mandated that no long-lived secrets exist anywhere in the deployment manifests, and the service also needs to enumerate the project's model deployments and connections at startup. How should the application connect to the Foundry project?
options: Instantiate AIProjectClient with the project endpoint and DefaultAzureCredential, backed by a workload identity that holds the appropriate Azure AI role on the project, then obtain inference clients from the project client
Keep the API key but move it into Azure Key Vault and fetch it at startup with a Key Vault SDK call using the pod's managed identity
Embed a service principal client ID and client secret in a Kubernetes secret and exchange them for a token at startup
Continue using the key, and rotate it automatically every 24 hours with a scheduled pipeline that updates the deployment manifest
optionExplanations: Correct. The project client is the entry point for project-scoped operations such as listing deployments and connections, and DefaultAzureCredential resolves the pod's workload identity in AKS and a developer's sign-in locally. Authorization comes from an Azure role assignment on the project, so there is no secret to store, rotate or leak.

This is better than an environment variable, but it is still key-based authentication: the key exists, can be exfiltrated from process memory or logs, and must be rotated. It also fails the stated requirement that no long-lived secret exists at all.

A client secret is precisely the long-lived credential the mandate prohibits, and storing it in a Kubernetes secret means it sits base64-encoded in etcd and in whatever manifests produced it. Managed identity exists to remove this class of credential.

Rotation shortens the exposure window but does not eliminate the secret, and writing keys into deployment manifests on a schedule spreads the credential through the pipeline and its logs. It also leaves the project-scoped operations without a clean authenticated client.
principle: connect with a project client and a managed identity, never a stored key
relatedConcept: Configuring an application to connect to a Foundry project means pointing a project client at the project endpoint and authenticating with Entra ID through DefaultAzureCredential and role assignments.
overallExplanation: Use the project client with the project endpoint and DefaultAzureCredential backed by workload identity. Keyless authentication satisfies the no-secrets mandate and the project client is what exposes deployments and connections to the app.

question: Your generative app reads the Azure AI Search endpoint and an admin key from application settings that were copied by hand when the index was created. The search service has since been recreated in a new resource group, three environments are now out of sync, and the same resource is already registered as a connection in the Foundry project. What is the cleanest way to make the app resilient to this?
options: Resolve the search resource at runtime from the Foundry project's connections, so the endpoint and authentication details come from the project rather than from copied app settings
Move the endpoint and admin key into Key Vault and reference them from app configuration in each environment
Hard-code the endpoint but read the admin key from an environment variable that the release pipeline injects per environment
Create a separate Azure AI Search service per environment and give each one a fixed, environment-specific naming convention the app can compute
optionExplanations: Correct. A project connection is the single registered definition of an external resource — endpoint plus authentication mode — so reading it at runtime means the app follows whatever the project points at. Recreating or repointing the search service updates one connection instead of three sets of copied settings.

Key Vault protects the secret but does not solve the drift: you now have three vault entries containing hand-copied endpoints and keys, and recreating the search service still means updating each one. The duplication of resource metadata is the actual problem.

This keeps the endpoint hard-coded, which is the value that changed when the resource moved, and it retains an admin key that a keyless connection would eliminate. Injecting it per environment institutionalizes the drift rather than removing it.

Naming conventions do not remove the copied credential and do not help when a resource is recreated in a different resource group or subscription. The app still holds its own private view of where the search service lives.
principle: external resources belong in project connections, not in copied app settings
relatedConcept: Foundry connections centralize endpoints and authentication for external resources such as Azure AI Search, storage and other services, so applications and agents resolve them by name.
overallExplanation: Resolve the search resource from the project's connections at runtime. Connections give one authoritative definition of the endpoint and its authentication, which removes per-environment copies of endpoints and admin keys.

question: Your team wants to run a four-week A/B test between two chat models from different providers in the Foundry model catalog, both deployed in the same project, and plans to swap in further candidates later. The current code calls the provider-specific SDK directly, so every candidate model requires a new client class, new message construction code and new tests. What should you adopt?
options: The Azure AI Inference SDK's chat completions client, which exposes a single, provider-neutral request and response shape across catalog model deployments
A provider-specific SDK for each candidate model, isolated behind a facade class that your application code calls
Direct REST calls built with an HTTP client, with a per-provider request template selected by configuration
One deployment per provider in a separate Foundry project, with traffic split by an Azure Front Door routing rule
optionExplanations: Correct. The inference SDK exists precisely for this: one chat completions surface with a common message, tool and response schema that works across model deployments from different providers in the catalog. Swapping a candidate becomes a configuration change of the deployment name rather than a new client implementation.

A hand-written facade can work but you are re-implementing, testing and maintaining the abstraction that the inference SDK already ships. Every new candidate still requires new adapter code, which is the cost the team is trying to eliminate.

Hand-rolled REST plus per-provider templates gives up typed clients, retry handling, telemetry integration and credential handling, and it fails the same way: each new provider means a new template and new tests.

Splitting providers across projects and routing at the edge complicates deployment, monitoring and quota management without touching the actual problem, which is provider-specific client code inside the application.
principle: a provider-neutral inference client makes model swaps a configuration change
relatedConcept: Foundry SDKs layer up: the project client resolves project resources and connections, and the inference client provides a uniform chat surface across catalog deployments.
overallExplanation: Use the provider-neutral Azure AI Inference chat client so candidate models differ only by deployment name. Writing your own facade or REST templates re-creates an abstraction the SDK already provides and keeps per-provider code in the app.

domain: Implement generative AI and agentic solutions
objective: Build generative applications by using Foundry
question: A claims-intake service asks a model to return an object with claim_number, incident_date, amount and injury_flag. About 6% of responses fail downstream parsing: some wrap the object in a markdown fence, some add an explanatory sentence, and some omit injury_flag when the narrative is ambiguous. The prompt already says "Respond with JSON only." What is the most reliable fix?
options: Set the response format to a JSON schema in strict mode, declaring the four fields and their types, so the service constrains decoding to that schema
Set the response format to JSON object mode, which forces the model to emit syntactically valid JSON
Add three worked examples of correctly formatted output to the prompt and repeat the "JSON only" instruction in the user message
Wrap the call in a parse-and-retry loop that reissues the request up to three times whenever json.loads raises an exception
optionExplanations: Correct. Schema-constrained decoding in strict mode enforces both the syntax and the shape: no markdown fence, no prose preamble, and no missing property, because tokens that would violate the schema cannot be produced. That covers all three observed failure classes rather than just the parse errors.

JSON object mode guarantees the output parses, which removes the fences and the prose, but it says nothing about which properties must be present. The ambiguous-narrative case that drops injury_flag would still produce valid JSON of the wrong shape.

Few-shot examples move the failure rate down but leave it stochastic, and they add tokens to every request. When a hard structural guarantee is available from the service, prompt persuasion is the weaker control.

Retrying catches syntax failures but not the silently missing field, which parses cleanly. It also multiplies latency and cost for the 6% of requests, and it treats a preventable formatting problem as a runtime error to be absorbed.
principle: constrain the output with a schema instead of asking the model to behave
relatedConcept: Structured output support ranges from free text, through JSON object mode which guarantees only syntax, to strict JSON schema mode which guarantees the shape of the object.
overallExplanation: Use strict JSON schema response format so the service constrains decoding to the declared shape. JSON object mode fixes only syntax, and prompt instructions or retries leave the missing-field case unaddressed.

domain: Implement generative AI and agentic solutions
objective: Build generative applications by using Foundry
question: A regression test asserts that a summarization endpoint returns byte-identical text for a fixed input. The team set temperature to 0, yet the test fails roughly once in every 30 runs with a response that differs by a word or two. Nothing else about the request changes between runs. How should the team handle this?
options: Treat temperature 0 as greedy sampling rather than a determinism guarantee — pass a fixed seed, track the returned system fingerprint, and assert on schema and semantic properties instead of byte equality
Also set top_p to 0, because determinism requires both sampling parameters to be pinned to their minimum values
Cache each response keyed by a hash of the prompt so that repeated identical requests always return the previously stored text
Fine-tune the model on the expected summaries so that the input reliably maps to a single memorized output
optionExplanations: Correct. Temperature 0 selects the highest-probability token but floating-point non-determinism, batching and backend model updates can still change a token here and there. A seed plus the system fingerprint gives you best-effort reproducibility and a signal when the backend changes, while assertions on structure and meaning make the test robust to harmless wording differences.

top_p and temperature are two ways of restricting the same sampling distribution, and pinning both does not remove the sources of variation described above. Setting top_p to 0 also risks degenerate behaviour on some deployments without buying the guarantee the team wants.

A cache makes the test pass by never exercising the model again, which defeats the purpose of a regression test. It also hides genuine model-behaviour regressions, which is exactly what this test exists to catch.

Fine-tuning to memorize outputs is enormously expensive relative to the problem, generalizes badly, and still does not guarantee identical decoding. It confuses making the model prefer an answer with making the runtime deterministic.
principle: temperature 0 is greedy decoding, not a determinism contract
relatedConcept: Tuning generation behaviour means understanding what each parameter actually controls: temperature and top_p shape the sampling distribution, while seed and system fingerprint provide best-effort reproducibility.
overallExplanation: Use a fixed seed, watch the system fingerprint, and assert on schema and meaning rather than exact bytes. Temperature 0 makes decoding greedy but never promises byte-identical responses across runs or backend updates.
